lead: Write Σa<sub>n</sub> for the infinite series with terms a<sub>n</sub>. Ordinary convergence asks whether its partial sums settle at one limit. Absolute convergence asks a stricter question: does the series of sizes Σ|a<sub>n</sub>| converge? The distinction matters because a convergent series can have positive and negative terms cancel, while its sizes may still add to infinity. That weaker case is conditional convergence. The idea is used when rearranging series, in Fourier series, and in numerical work where the order of terms can change the computed sum.
prereq: You need: 3.2 for series and partial sums, 3.3 for positive-term tests, and 3.4 for alternating series.

blocks.text: Let Σan be a series with real terms an. The series is absolutely convergent when Σ|an| converges. The same series is conditionally convergent when Σan converges but Σ|an| diverges. Some books write “Σan converges absolutely” instead of “Σan is absolutely convergent”. Absolute convergence is stronger: it controls the sizes of all terms, not just their signed sum.

The main theorem: if Σ|a<sub>n</sub>| converges, then Σa<sub>n</sub> converges. Reason: for any tail from m to N, |a<sub>m</sub>+⋯+a<sub>N</sub>| ≤ |a<sub>m</sub>|+⋯+|a<sub>N</sub>|. If Σ|a<sub>n</sub>| converges, those positive tails become small, so the partial sums of Σa<sub>n</sub> have a real limit. The converse is false.

blocks.where: a<sub>n</sub> are real terms; |a<sub>n</sub>| is the absolute value; the arrow means “implies”.

blocks.text: The standard counterexample is the alternating harmonic series Σ(−1)n+1/n. It converges by the Leibnitz test: the sizes 1/n decrease to 0. Its absolute version is the harmonic series Σ1/n, which diverges (p=1). Therefore the alternating harmonic series is convergent but not absolutely convergent, so it is conditionally convergent. Two absolutely convergent examples: Σ1/n² (p=2) and Σ1/2n, which is geometric with ratio 1/2 and so converges. Read Σ1/2n as Σ(1/2)n. The different series Σ1/(2n) is half the harmonic series and diverges.

sections.h3: How to test a signed series

blocks.text: Do not start with the signs. First make every term positive by taking |an|, then apply the tests from 3.3: comparison, integral, ratio or root. If Σ|an| converges, stop: the original Σan is absolutely convergent, and therefore convergent.

items: Form A<sub>N</sub> = Σ<sub>n=1</sub><sup>N</sup> |a<sub>n</sub>| and decide whether A<sub>N</sub> has a finite limit using 3.3.
If A<sub>N</sub> converges, the original series is absolutely convergent. No further sign test is needed.
If A<sub>N</sub> diverges, the original may still converge. Test Σa<sub>n</sub> itself, often with the alternating test in 3.4 when the signs alternate.
If the original converges and the absolute series diverges, label it conditionally convergent. If the original also diverges, label it divergent.

blocks.text: A p-series Σ1/n<sup>p</sup> converges for p>1 and diverges for p≤1. A shift such as 1/√(n+1) does not change p. Ratio test limit L=1 is inconclusive, so switch to another test; do not guess.

For a finite sum, order does not matter: 1−1/2+1/3 and 1/3−1/2+1 are the same. For infinite conditionally convergent series, order can matter. The Riemann rearrangement theorem says: if Σa<sub>n</sub> converges conditionally and S is any real number (or ±∞), then some rearrangement of its terms has sum S. We state it only; the proof belongs with later analysis. Absolutely convergent series are safe: every rearrangement has the same sum.

This is the practical reason to test absolute convergence first. If a series is absolutely convergent, you may regroup and reorder terms as if it were a finite sum. If it is only conditionally convergent, keep the given order unless the problem explicitly asks about rearrangements. The usual alternating harmonic series sums to ln 2, but a rearrangement can change that sum. Power series use absolute convergence inside the radius of convergence; see 3.6.

figure.caption: Nested sets: the whole circle is all convergent series; the inner circle is absolutely convergent series. The alternating harmonic series lies in the outer ring only.

spec.aria: Nested sets place absolutely convergent series inside all convergent series, with the alternating harmonic series in the outer ring.

examples.question: Classify the series Σ<sub>n=1</sub><sup>∞</sup> (−1)<sup>n</sup>/√(n+1) as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent. Name each test you use and give the p-value of the comparison series.
steps: The absolute series is Σ<sub>n=1</sub><sup>∞</sup> 1/(n+1)<sup>1/2</sup>. Shift m = n+1 to get Σ<sub>m=2</sub><sup>∞</sup> 1/m<sup>1/2</sup>. This is a p-series with p = 1/2 = 0.5. Since p ≤ 1, it diverges. Hence the original series is not absolutely convergent.

The original series is alternating because (−1)<sup>n</sup> flips sign. Put b<sub>n</sub> = 1/√(n+1) > 0. As n increases, n+1 increases, √(n+1) increases, so b<sub>n</sub> decreases. Also b<sub>n</sub> → 0 as n → ∞.
By the Leibnitz test in 3.4, Σa<sub>n</sub> converges. It converges but its absolute series diverges, so it is conditionally convergent.
examples.answer: The series is conditionally convergent: it converges by the Leibnitz test, but its absolute series has p=1/2=0.5 and diverges.

traps: Do not write “convergent” when the question asks “absolutely convergent”. Every absolutely convergent series converges, but the converse fails for Σ(−1)<sup>n+1</sup>/n.
If Σ|a<sub>n</sub>| diverges, the original Σa<sub>n</sub> may still converge. The correct label can be conditionally convergent.
Do not apply the alternating series test to Σ|a<sub>n</sub>|; all its terms are positive. Use positive-term tests first.
A shift in the index does not change a p-series exponent: Σ1/√(n+1) has p=1/2 and diverges, just like Σ1/√n.
Only absolutely convergent series may be rearranged freely. A conditionally convergent series can change its sum under rearrangement.

quiz.a: Σa<sub>n</sub> is absolutely convergent when Σ|a<sub>n</sub>| converges.

quiz.q: True or false: every convergent series is absolutely convergent. Give a counterexample.
quiz.a: False. The alternating harmonic series Σ(−1)<sup>n+1</sup>/n converges by the Leibnitz test, but Σ1/n diverges, so it is not absolutely convergent.
Take absolute values: Σ1/n<sup>3</sup> is a p-series with p=3>1, so it converges. The original series is absolutely convergent.

The absolute series Σ1/(n+1) is a shifted harmonic series, so it diverges. The original is alternating with b<sub>n</sub>=1/(n+1) decreasing to 0, so it converges by the Leibnitz test. Hence it is conditionally convergent.

quiz.q: A student applies the ratio test to Σ|a<sub>n</sub>| and gets L=1. What can be concluded, and what should be done next?
quiz.a: The ratio test is inconclusive. Use another positive-term test such as comparison, integral, or root. If the absolute series diverges, test the original signed series, often by the alternating test.

quiz.q: State what the Riemann rearrangement theorem says for a conditionally convergent series. Does it apply to Σ1/n<sup>2</sup>?
quiz.a: For a conditionally convergent series, any real sum S can be obtained by some rearrangement of its terms. It does not apply to Σ1/n<sup>2</sup>, because that series is absolutely convergent and all rearrangements have the same sum.

quiz.q: Why does Σ|a<sub>n</sub>| convergence force Σa<sub>n</sub> convergence? Use one inequality.
quiz.a: For a tail, |a<sub>m</sub>+⋯+a<sub>N</sub>| ≤ |a<sub>m</sub>|+⋯+|a<sub>N</sub>|. The right side becomes small because Σ|a<sub>n</sub>| converges, so the partial sums of Σa<sub>n</sub> settle at a real limit.

quiz.q: Which is absolutely convergent: Σ(−1)<sup>n</sup>/n<sup>2</sup> or Σ(−1)<sup>n</sup>/n? Give the reason.
quiz.a: Σ(−1)<sup>n</sup>/n<sup>2</sup> is absolutely convergent because Σ1/n<sup>2</sup> has p=2>1. Σ(−1)<sup>n</sup>/n is only conditionally convergent because Σ1/n diverges.

beyond: Not for the exam. Absolute convergence is the dividing line between series you can treat like finite sums and series that depend on order, which matters in Fourier series and in numerical summation where round-off reorders terms. In analysis, the same idea appears for integrals and for series in Banach spaces. In machine learning, conditionally convergent expansions are handled with care. Search next: Riemann rearrangement theorem, unconditional convergence, rearrangement of series.
